reasoning: The row was admitted on a narrow definition of done — a run naming an act on a no-act scenario must fail — and a row is closed against the DOD it was admitted on. That DOD is met and its unit test passes. What is not finished is the delivery: the shared branch the fix landed in also governs the extra-act case, and the verifier's closing check reaches the product on real data — the 35 recorded runs — where it reads 26 instead of 30, four of them red on every-other-field-right runs. That is a red check inside what this change touched, so the pipeline does not close over it; it splits the two cases apart, which the situation says is possible, and re-verifies. But the repair needs no word from the person: the eval's written cost model already states what the wider case should do — print a note, not a failure — so this is not a product choice no artifact settles, not taste, and not an open fork in the definition of correct; the artifact settles it, and the pipeline reads it rather than asking. The over-reach is exactly the flaw the pipeline is obliged to state plainly (the delivered code contradicts a standing decision already on record) and then handle, not a reason to stall, and the class-hunt duty makes sweeping the sibling case part of the same piece of work rather than a new question. Nothing here is irreversible outside git, and the person's eye is never the gate on an ordinary buildable result a command already confirms. So the pipeline finishes the split, verifies the 35 runs back to 30 with a receipt not from the row's holder, shows the result and closes in the same step; if he later disagrees with the split, that is a new fact and a new row, not a reopening.
